serverBlurb: Which PostgreSQL this is, who this service connects as, and how big the database has become.
activityHeading: What it has done, and who is connected
activityBlurb: Every counter PostgreSQL keeps for this database, the backends on it, and the locks they hold.
backgroundBlurb: The writer, the checkpointer, the write-ahead log and the archiver. Three of these four views moved or arrived between major versions, which is why this page asks each of them for every column rather than naming any.
schemaBlurb: Per-table and per-index statistics, sizes, columns and constraints — scoped to current_schema(), so an operator who moved the schema in their connection string gets their own tables rather than somebody else's.
configBlurb: Every setting an operator changed from its built-in default — PostgreSQL's own answer to "what did somebody set" — plus a named handful that matter whether or not anybody touched them.
noView: This server version does not have that view.
viewArrived: It arrived in PostgreSQL {version}, so this is the ordinary answer on anything older and not a fault.
mayNotRead: This service's database role may not read it. Granting pg_monitor to that role is what fills it in; this service does not ask for it.
noRow: That view answered no row at all, which for a probe scoped to this database means the server keeps no statistics for it yet.
wouldShow: What this page would show: everything PostgreSQL keeps about itself — commits and rollbacks, the cache hit ratio, every backend and lock, the checkpointer and the write-ahead log — beside per-table and per-index statistics for the schema this service owns, its sizes, its columns and its constraints.
wouldShowAfter: is where the mode is configured and is what this page reports the consequences of.
noDatabaseTitle: There is no database to report on
whatDoing: This page is what the database has been DOING.
whatConfigured: , under Settings, is what this service is CONFIGURED to write down and where — that page reads the same on a service that started a second ago, and the numbers here move while you watch.
whatShape: The shape of this page is decided by the database it is pointed at. Every statement behind it is a SELECT *, and the columns drawn are the ones this server returned, in its order. That is not laziness: PostgreSQL moves these views between major versions — pg_stat_bgwriter has eleven columns on 16 and four on 18, because the checkpoint counters moved to a view that does not exist before 17 — so a page naming its columns would be wrong on every server but one, and wrong in the way that reads as a blank cell.
whatNoQuery: There is no query box here and there must never be one. The role this service dials with can INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on six tables, so a console that could hand it a statement would be a console that could empty the directory. Every statement is a literal in persistence/persistence_postgres.js and none is built from anything a request carries. They are all catalog reads, bounded by PostgreSQL's own statement_timeout at {ms}ms
timeoutNotInForce: — which this server would not accept, so that bound is NOT in force
singleConnection: , on the single connection this page borrows.
whatTitle: What this page is, and the three things it will not do
poolFigures: The pool figures are this PROCESS's and the backend counts are the SERVER's, and they answer different questions: PostgreSQL can say how many connections exist, and only the client can say how many of them this service is holding and how many callers are queued for one. The pool is sampled BEFORE this page borrows a connection, so the numbers are what it was doing when you asked rather than what it is doing because you asked — on a pool whose maximum is four, counting our own would invent a quarter of it.
connectionTitle: Which end each number comes from
narrowedRole: This service connects as an ordinary application role — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on six tables, USAGE on one schema, and not pg_monitor. Most of what is below is readable by anybody; two things are not, and they fail differently:
narrowedView: a view this role may not read fails, and is drawn as a row in What could not be collected with PostgreSQL's SQLSTATE beside it;
narrowedBackend: a backend belonging to another role does not fail — it appears as a row with its state empty and its query given as the literal string <insufficient privilege>, which is a value and not an error. This page draws that as withheld. The same is true of pg_stat_replication: an empty table there means either that there are no standbys or that this role may not see them, and nothing in this service can tell those apart.
narrowedGrant: Granting pg_monitor to the application role fills all of it in. This service does not ask for it, because the whole point of postgres/schema.sql is that the role it dials with holds the least it can.
narrowedTitle: What this role is NOT allowed to see, and how each kind of refusal looks
unusedWhy: . On a database that has been serving traffic that is the most actionable number on this page — an index nothing reads is write cost and disk for nothing. On one that has just started it means only that nothing has queried yet, and the counters below say which situation this is.
allScanned: Every index here has been scanned at least once.
cacheHitWhy: Blocks found in the buffer cache against blocks read from disk. PostgreSQL keeps the two counters and not the ratio, because a counter can be subtracted between two readings and a ratio cannot.
rollbacksWhy: A share and not a count: rollbacks are ordinary here — a conflicting upsert produces one — and only the proportion means anything.
deadTuplesWhy: Dead rows as a share of all rows, summed across the schema. This is the bloat signal; autovacuum is what brings it down, and the per-table vacuum times are in the schema section.
scansWhy: On six small tables a sequential scan is frequently the right plan and this is not a fault to chase — read it beside the row counts below.
cumulativeSince: Every figure on this page is cumulative since {since}
cumulativeSinceReset: Every figure on this page is cumulative since the statistics were last reset
cumulativeWhy: , which is what PostgreSQL counts from. A cache hit ratio over the life of a server says nothing about the last hour, and reading it as a current figure is the one misunderstanding this page can actually cause.
ratiosTitle: Four numbers this page computes, and what each is not
missingHead: {n} object(s) this service's driver declares are NOT in the database:
missingWhy: The driver creates what is missing when it opens — and on a least-privilege deployment it cannot, because the role it dials with holds no CREATE. There the failure arrives as a permission error naming a statement nobody typed. Re-run postgres/schema.sql as the owner.
missingTitle: The schema is missing something the driver expects
allPresent: All {n} objects the driver declares are present, at schema version {version}.
onlyCheck: Nothing else in this service makes this check. tests/postgres_schema.js compares the driver against postgres/schema.sql character for character, and neither of those is ever compared against a running server — so a database built by an older copy of that file, or by hand, or half-migrated, satisfies both and is missing a table.
reverseNot: The reverse is deliberately not reported: a table in this schema the driver never heard of is an operator's business, and a page calling it an error would be this service claiming a namespace it does not own.
presentTitle: The schema is what the driver expects
allAnswered: Nothing. Every one of the {n} probes answered.
someFailed: {failed} of {total} probes did not answer. Each one costs a row here rather than the page, which is why they are run and caught separately: which views a role may read depends on the server version and on the operator's grants, and one rejection must not take the other nineteen with it.
